title: General Wave Properties
seo_title: Secondary 3 Physics: General Wave Properties Worksheets (O-Level 6091 with Answers)
standard_text: Describe what is meant by wave motion and show understanding that waves transfer energy without transferring matter; define speed, frequency, wavelength, period and amplitude and recall and apply v = fλ; compare transverse and longitudinal waves; interpret displacement-distance and displacement-time graphs; describe sound as a longitudinal wave made of compressions and rarefactions that needs a medium; compare the speed of sound in solids, liquids and gases; describe echoes and the use of ultrasound; relate loudness to amplitude and pitch to frequency (summary of the Singapore-Cambridge O-Level Physics 6091 syllabus).
meta_desc: Free Secondary 3 O-Level Physics worksheets on general wave properties: transverse and longitudinal waves, amplitude, wavelength, frequency, v = fλ, wave graphs, sound, echoes and ultrasound. 100 questions with answers.
body_html:
How to think about it

A wave transfers energy without transferring matter.

  • Transverse waves (light, water ripples) vibrate at right angles to the direction of travel; longitudinal waves (sound) vibrate along it.
  • v = fλ and f = 1 ÷ T. Amplitude is measured from the rest position.
  • Sound needs a medium: fastest in solids, slowest in gases, none in a vacuum (about 340 m/s in air). For an echo, distance = speed × time ÷ 2.
  • Larger amplitude: louder. Higher frequency: higher pitch. Humans hear about 20 Hz to 20 kHz; above that is ultrasound.
Example

f = 50 Hz, λ = 0.4 m. Speed?

v = 50 × 0.4

Answer: 20 m/s

Example

An echo returns after 1.5 s (v = 340 m/s). Distance to the wall?

2d = 340 × 1.5 = 510

d = 510 ÷ 2

Answer: 255 m

Common mistakes

  • Measuring the amplitude from crest to trough. It is from the middle line to a crest.
  • Forgetting to halve the distance in echo questions.
  • Saying sound is fastest in air. It is fastest in solids.
  • Mixing up pitch (frequency) and loudness (amplitude).

faq.a: v = fλ: wave speed (m/s) = frequency (Hz) × wavelength (m). Also f = 1 ÷ T.

faq.q: What is the difference between transverse and longitudinal waves?
faq.a: In transverse waves the particles vibrate at right angles to the direction the wave travels; in longitudinal waves they vibrate along that direction.

faq.q: How do you find a distance from an echo?
faq.a: Multiply the speed of sound by the echo time to get the distance there and back, then divide by 2.

items.q: Which change to a sound wave gives a higher pitch?
items.e: A higher frequency: a higher pitch.

items.q: Is this a transverse or a longitudinal wave: water ripples?
c: neither: it is not a wave
items.e: Transverse: vibration at right angles to travel. Longitudinal: vibration along the direction of travel.

items.q: Is this a transverse or a longitudinal wave: sound waves?
c: neither: it is not a wave
items.e: Transverse: vibration at right angles to travel. Longitudinal: vibration along the direction of travel.

items.q: What is the frequency of a wave?
c: the number of complete waves produced per second

items.q: Why can sound not travel through outer space?
c: Space is a vacuum with no particles to pass on the vibrations.

items.q: Is sound a transverse or a longitudinal wave?
items.e: Transverse: vibrations at right angles to the direction of energy transfer. Longitudinal: vibrations parallel to it.

items.q: Is this a transverse or a longitudinal wave: it has crests and troughs?
c: neither: it is not a wave
items.e: Transverse: vibration at right angles to travel. Longitudinal: vibration along the direction of travel.

items.q: Is this a transverse or a longitudinal wave: the vibrations are parallel to the direction of wave travel?
c: neither: it is not a wave
items.e: Transverse: vibration at right angles to travel. Longitudinal: vibration along the direction of travel.

items.q: What do waves transfer?
items.e: A cork on a pond bobs up and down but stays in place.

items.q: Is this a transverse or a longitudinal wave: waves on a slinky pushed back and forth along its length?
c: neither: it is not a wave
items.e: Transverse: vibration at right angles to travel. Longitudinal: vibration along the direction of travel.

items.q: Which change to a sound wave gives a louder sound?
items.e: A larger amplitude: a louder sound.

items.q: What is the amplitude of a wave?
c: the number of waves per second
the maximum displacement of a point from its rest position
the distance from crest to trough

items.q: Are S-waves in an earthquake transverse or longitudinal waves?
items.e: Transverse: vibrations at right angles to the direction of energy transfer. Longitudinal: vibrations parallel to it.

items.q: What is the period of a wave?
c: the number of waves per second
the distance travelled in one second
the time taken to produce one complete wave

items.q: What is a wavefront?
c: a line joining points on a wave that are in phase, such as all the crests
the front edge of the water
the fastest part of a wave
items.e: Wavefronts are perpendicular to the direction of travel.

items.q: Are waves on a guitar string transverse or longitudinal waves?
items.e: Transverse: vibrations at right angles to the direction of energy transfer. Longitudinal: vibrations parallel to it.

items.q: Is this a transverse or a longitudinal wave: the vibrations are perpendicular to the direction of wave travel?
c: neither: it is not a wave
items.e: Transverse: vibration at right angles to travel. Longitudinal: vibration along the direction of travel.

items.q: What does a smaller amplitude of a sound wave give?
items.e: A smaller amplitude: a softer sound.

items.q: Is this a transverse or a longitudinal wave: ultrasound?
c: neither: it is not a wave
items.e: Transverse: vibration at right angles to travel. Longitudinal: vibration along the direction of travel.

items.q: Are ripples on water transverse or longitudinal waves?
items.e: Transverse: vibrations at right angles to the direction of energy transfer. Longitudinal: vibrations parallel to it.

items.q: What is the wavelength of a wave?
c: the distance from crest to trough
the shortest distance between two points in phase, such as two neighbouring crests

items.e: Amplitude = maximum displacement from the rest position = 1 cm.

items.q: What is a compression in a sound wave?
c: a region where particles are far apart
a region where the air particles are closer together and the pressure is higher
items.e: Rarefactions are where particles are further apart.

items.q: Is this a transverse or a longitudinal wave: light waves?
c: neither: it is not a wave
items.e: Transverse: vibration at right angles to travel. Longitudinal: vibration along the direction of travel.

items.q: What is the range of frequencies a healthy young person can hear?
Is this a transverse or a longitudinal wave: it has compressions and rarefactions?
c: neither: it is not a wave
items.e: Transverse: vibration at right angles to travel. Longitudinal: vibration along the direction of travel.

items.q: What is ultrasound?
c: sound with a frequency above 20 000 Hz
sound that travels faster than light
items.e: Used in medical scans and sonar.

items.q: A student claps near a wall and hears the echo 1.2 s later. Sound travels at 340 m/s. How far away is the wall?
items.e: The sound goes there and back: 340 × 1.2 = 408 m, so the wall is 204 m away.

items.q: A student claps in front of a tall wall and hears the echo 0.3 s later. The speed of sound in air is 340 m/s. How far away is the wall?
items.e: Sound travels to the wall and back: 2d = 340 × 0.3, so d = 51 m.

items.q: A wall is 34 m away. How long after a shout is the echo heard? (speed of sound = 340 m/s)
A student claps near a wall and hears the echo 1 s later. Sound travels at 340 m/s. How far away is the wall?
items.e: The sound goes there and back: 340 × 1 = 340 m, so the wall is 170 m away.

items.q: A ringing bell is placed in a jar and the air is pumped out. What happens to the sound heard?
c: It becomes fainter until it can hardly be heard.
items.e: Sound cannot travel through a vacuum.

items.q: In which of these does sound travel slowest: steel, concrete, water or air?
items.e: Gas particles are far apart, so vibrations pass on slowly.

items.q: A ship's sonar sends an ultrasound pulse to the seabed. The echo returns after 1.2 s. Sound travels at 1500 m/s in seawater. How deep is the sea?
items.e: Distance there and back = 1500 × 1.2 = 1800 m; depth = half = 900 m.

items.q: A student claps near a wall and hears the echo 0.5 s later. Sound travels at 330 m/s. How far away is the wall?
items.e: The sound goes there and back: 330 × 0.5 = 165 m, so the wall is 82 m away.

items.q: What does a larger amplitude of a sound wave give?
items.e: A larger amplitude: a louder sound.

items.q: A student stands 68 m from a cliff. The echo of her clap is heard 0.4 s later. What is the speed of sound?
A student claps in front of a tall wall and hears the echo 0.4 s later. The speed of sound in air is 340 m/s. How far away is the wall?
items.e: Sound travels to the wall and back: 2d = 340 × 0.4, so d = 68 m.

items.q: What does a lower frequency of a sound wave give?
items.e: A lower frequency: a lower pitch.

items.q: Sound travels at 340 m/s in air. How far does sound travel in 1.5 s?
A ship's sonar sends an ultrasound pulse to the seabed. The echo returns after 0.4 s. Sound travels at 1500 m/s in seawater. How deep is the sea?
items.e: Distance there and back = 1500 × 0.4 = 600 m; depth = half = 300 m.

items.q: Why does sound travel faster in solids than in gases?
c: The particles are closer together, so vibrations are passed on more quickly.

items.q: In which medium does sound travel fastest: air, water, steel or a vacuum?
items.e: Sound is fastest in solids, slower in liquids, slowest in gases, and cannot travel in a vacuum.

items.q: A student claps in front of a tall wall and hears the echo 0.5 s later. The speed of sound in air is 340 m/s. How far away is the wall?
items.e: Sound travels to the wall and back: 2d = 340 × 0.5, so d = 85 m.

items.q: What does a higher frequency of a sound wave give?
items.e: A higher frequency: a higher pitch.

items.q: A ship's sonar sends an ultrasound pulse to the seabed. The echo returns after 0.2 s. Sound travels at 1500 m/s in seawater. How deep is the sea?
items.e: Distance there and back = 1500 × 0.2 = 300 m; depth = half = 150 m.

items.q: A student watches a firework 680 m away. How long after the flash does she hear the bang? (speed of sound = 340 m/s)
items.e: Light arrives almost at once; t = 680 ÷ 340.

items.q: A wave's frequency doubles while its speed stays the same. What happens to its wavelength?
c: It becomes four times as long.

items.q: A cork floats on a pond as ripples pass. How does it move?
c: along with the ripples to the edge
up and down, staying in about the same place
in a circle across the pond
items.e: The water does not travel with the wave.

items.q: Why is an echo not heard from a wall only 5 m away?
c: The wall absorbs all the sound.
The echo returns too quickly (in about 0.03 s) to be heard separately from the original sound.
items.e: The ear needs about 0.1 s between sounds.

items.q: A sound wave in air travels at 340 m/s with a frequency of 250 Hz. What is its wavelength?
A water wave in a ripple tank travels at 0.06 m/s with a wavelength of 0.015 m. What is its frequency?

items.e: One complete wave (crest to crest) spans 20 cm.

items.q: A guitar string is plucked harder. What changes?
c: The amplitude increases, so the sound is louder.
items.e: Pitch depends on frequency, loudness on amplitude.

items.q: A ship's sonar sends an ultrasound pulse to the seabed. The echo returns after 0.8 s. Sound travels at 1500 m/s in seawater. How deep is the sea?
items.e: Distance there and back = 1500 × 0.8 = 1200 m; depth = half = 600 m.

items.e: Echoes from tissue boundaries build up an image.
